blocks.text: A fraction needs a reference unit. If we speak of half a sheet of paper, the unit is one sheet; if we speak of half a liter, the unit is one liter. Before counting parts, decide what represents the whole. Two pieces can be the same size as each other yet be halves of sheets of different sizes. A fractional number compares each part with its own whole; it does not guarantee that the parts have the same length or area.

In \(\frac{3}{5}\), the denominator 5 means the whole is divided into five equal parts. The numerator 3 tells us how many of those parts we take. Equal-sized parts are essential: choosing three pieces from an irregularly cut object does not mean that we chose three fifths. We are not merely counting pieces; we are counting fractional units of the same size.

Imagine a one-meter rope divided into five equal segments. Each segment measures one fifth of a meter. Three segments measure three fifths. Five segments make one meter, and eight segments measure eight fifths of a meter, even if we must continue onto another identical rope. A fraction need not be less than one: the numerator may equal or exceed the denominator.

blocks.prompt: A bar is cut into four pieces. One is half the bar, and the other three share the remaining half equally. One of those three smaller pieces is chosen. Which statement is justified?

options.label: It is one quarter because there are four pieces.
options.reviewFeedback: Your explanation counts all pieces as though they were the same size. Review the equal-parts condition before using the number of pieces as the denominator.

options.label: It is one sixth because the three smaller pieces share one half.
options.reviewFeedback: Check which whole quantity serves as the unit and how the smaller pieces divide that whole.

options.label: It is one third of the bar because there are three smaller pieces.
options.reviewFeedback: Your argument counts the smaller pieces but must specify what quantity they share. Distinguish a fraction of half the bar from a fraction of the entire bar.

feedback.correct: Half of the bar is split into three equal parts: six of those small pieces would make a whole bar. Each is one sixth.
feedback.incorrect: Pieces of different sizes cannot be counted as equal fractional units. Identify the whole and the equal parts within it.

blocks.text: Quotients, Improper Fractions, and Mixed Numbers

A fraction can also describe sharing: three meters shared equally among five people give three fifths of a meter per person. We can divide each meter into fifths and give three of those pieces to each person. The denominator cannot be zero: 'sharing among zero people' does not determine an amount per person.

To convert a fraction greater than one into a mixed-number expression, separate the whole units. For example, \(\frac{13}{4}=\frac{12}{4}+\frac{1}{4}=3+\frac{1}{4}\). We read this as three and one quarter. Here the plus sign makes the relationship unambiguous. To return to a fraction, each whole contributes four quarters: three wholes and one quarter make thirteen quarters.

Integer division helps organize this calculation. Dividing thirteen by four gives quotient three and remainder one. The remainder counts the quarters left over, so the denominator stays four. We do not write three thirds or interpret the remainder as one tenth. Every representation describes the same point on the number line.

blocks.prompt: There are nine segments, each one fifth of a meter long. Write their total length as a number. An equivalent fraction is accepted.

feedback.correct: Nine fifths are 9/5 of a meter: one whole uses five segments and four fifths remain. The answer lies between one and two meters.
feedback.incorrect: The denominator remains five because each segment is one fifth. Keep the number of segments distinct from the size of each segment.

blocks.prompt: A container holds two complete liters plus another three quarters of a liter. What number expresses its total volume in liters?

feedback.correct: Two liters are eight quarters. Eight quarters plus three quarters make eleven quarters: 11/4 L.
feedback.incorrect: First convert two whole units to eight quarters, then add the remaining three quarters. The result should lie between two and three liters.

blocks.text: Changing the physical reference unit can change the amount represented by the same fraction. Half of a ten-meter rope is five meters; half of a six-meter rope is three. To compare quantities, keep the same unit or convert to a common one. To compare numbers on the number line, use the same zero and the same zero-to-one interval.

blocks.prompt: Seven liters of water are shared equally among four empty containers. How many liters does each container receive? Mentally check that four portions reconstruct all seven liters.

feedback.correct: Each receives 7/4 L. Giving one liter to each uses four liters; the remaining three liters add another three quarters of a liter per container.
feedback.incorrect: The total is divided by the number of containers. The portion must be greater than one liter and less than two, and all four portions must reconstruct seven liters.

blocks.prompt: The interval from zero to one is one unit, and each space between marks represents one quarter. Which fraction corresponds to the marked point?

feedback.correct: The mark is nine quarters from zero: eight quarters complete two units, with one quarter remaining. Its value is 9/4.
feedback.incorrect: Count intervals starting from zero. The point is beyond two whole units, so check the number of quarters that have elapsed.

blocks.prompt: Lina takes half of a 12 m ribbon. Oscar takes one third of another, 24 m long. Who takes a greater length?

options.label: Lina, because 1/2 is greater than 1/3.
options.reviewFeedback: Your argument compares the fractions without considering the lengths of the whole ribbons. Calculate each portion using its own reference whole.

options.label: Oscar: he takes 8 m, while Lina takes 6 m.
options.reviewFeedback: Check that the lengths in your chosen statement follow from the given ribbons and that both use the same measurement unit.

options.label: Both, because each takes a fraction of a ribbon.
options.reviewFeedback: Taking a part of a ribbon describes an operation but does not determine a length by itself. Review which reference whole applies to each portion.

feedback.correct: Oscar takes 24 ÷ 3 = 8 m; Lina takes 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m. A smaller fraction can give a greater length when the whole is larger.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the actual lengths using the same unit. Fractions of different-sized wholes cannot be compared as physical quantities from the fractions alone.

blocks.text: Reconstruct the Whole and Change Representations

If three parts, each a fifth, measure 12 cm altogether, each fifth measures 4 cm and the whole is 20 cm. A fraction expresses a relationship with the whole; knowing part of the whole lets us reconstruct it. We do not multiply 12 by five, because 12 cm represents three parts, not one.

blocks.prompt: Four sixths of a uniform ribbon measure 18 cm. How long is one sixth, and how long is the entire ribbon?

feedback.correct: Each sixth measures 18/4 = 9/2 cm. All six sixths measure 27 cm; four of them reproduce the given 18 cm.
feedback.incorrect: Dividing or multiplying directly by six ignores that 18 cm is the length of four sixths. First find the length of one of those four known parts.

blocks.text: Division with remainder gives two expressions for the same number. In 17/6 there are two whole units and five sixths: 17 = 2×6+5. The remainder must be less than six, because six sixths would make another whole unit.

blocks.prompt: Write 23/5 as whole units plus a proper fraction. Enter the number of whole units and the numerator of the remaining fifths.

feedback.correct: 23 = 4×5+3, so 23/5 = 4+3/5. Four whole units contain twenty fifths.
feedback.incorrect: The remainder is the number of fifths still left after forming the whole units. Keep the denominator five.

blocks.prompt: Each tile measures 1/8 m. Complete the lengths of both sets; they use the same meter as the unit.

feedback.correct: Three tiles measure 3/8 m; ten measure 10/8 = 5/4 m. Eight tiles make one meter.
feedback.incorrect: The denominator eight gives the size of each tile and stays unchanged as the tiles are counted. Do not interchange the number of tiles and the size of a part.

blocks.prompt: Two liters are shared equally among seven containers. Write the liters per container and choose a way to check your answer.

options.label: Each container receives more than one liter because seven is greater than two.
options.reviewFeedback: Your reasoning uses the number of containers to justify the size of a portion. Consider how a fixed total changes when divided among more containers.

options.label: Multiplying the liters in one portion by the number of containers recovers two liters.
options.reviewFeedback: Check that your method relates one portion to the total number of containers and keeps liters as the unit.

options.label: Two portions of 7/2 L reconstruct the two liters.
options.reviewFeedback: Your check uses a different number of portions than the one described. Review the roles of the total and the number of containers before reversing a division.

feedback.correct: Each container receives 2/7 L. Seven portions of 2/7 L make 2 L, and each portion is less than one liter.
feedback.incorrect: A correct portion, multiplied by seven containers, must recover the given two-liter total. Compare the size of each portion with one liter.

blocks.prompt: Two boxes contain 30 and 18 counters. Take 1/3 of the first and 1/2 of the second. Enter both amounts and choose which is greater.

options.label: The second, because 1/2 > 1/3.
options.reviewFeedback: This reasoning compares only the fractions. Consider the number of counters in the chosen box before calculating the size of that fraction.

options.label: They are equal because both are parts of boxes.
options.reviewFeedback: Your reasoning assumes that parts from different boxes represent equal quantities. Check whether the complete boxes contain the same number of counters.

options.label: The first: when both portions are expressed in counters, the first is greater.
options.reviewFeedback: Check that both amounts are calculated using the fraction and total of their respective boxes. Keep counters as the unit of comparison.

feedback.correct: One third of thirty is ten counters; half of eighteen is nine. The reference wholes have different sizes.
feedback.incorrect: Comparing only 1/3 and 1/2 does not compare the actual numbers of counters. Calculate both quantities in counters first.

blocks.prompt: One team receives zero meters; another receives twelve meters shared among four people. Write the amount received by one person on the second team.

feedback.correct: 12/4 = 3. A fraction can also represent a whole number; 3 = 3/1.
feedback.incorrect: Divide the twelve meters among the four people in the second team. The zero received by the other team does not affect this calculation.
